pages.x: Lisbon was one of the richest cities in Europe, capital of an empire that reached Brazil, Africa and India. On the morning of 1 November 1755, All Saints' Day, its churches were full for Mass, with candles burning on every altar.

At about 9.40 the ground shook for several minutes, in one of the strongest earthquakes ever known in Europe. Churches, palaces and houses fell on the people inside, and great cracks opened in the streets.
Survivors fled to the open waterfront and saw the sea drain away, showing wrecks on the harbour floor. Then a tsunami swept in. Fires started by the candles burned for five days.

pages.t: Bury the dead, heal the living
pages.x: When the king asked what to do, his minister, later the Marquis of Pombal, is said to have answered: bury the dead and heal the living. He had the ruins cleared, food prices fixed and looters hanged, and rebuilt the centre with wide, straight streets.
Pombal's engineers gave the new buildings a flexible wooden cage inside the walls, and tested it by marching soldiers around a model to shake it.
pages.fx: It was one of the first earthquake-proof designs in the world, and the Baixa district built that way still stands.

pages.x: Pombal sent every parish a list of questions: how long did the shaking last, did the sea rise, how many buildings fell? The answers are still studied, and he is sometimes called the father of the science of earthquakes.

pages.t: The best of all possible worlds?
pages.x: The disaster shook thinkers across Europe. If God was good, why would he kill thousands of people at prayer on a holy day? Voltaire wrote a poem about it, and later Candide, which mocks the idea that all is for the best in this best of all possible worlds.

The Lisbon earthquake was one of the deadliest in history. It led to the first rebuilding with earthquake-proof design and the first scientific study of an earthquake, and pushed European thinkers to look for natural, not divine, causes of disaster.
